title: BATAYAN: A Filipino NLP benchmark for evaluating Large Language Models
problem_statement: Large language models demonstrate high performance on major high-resource languages, but under-resourced languages such as Filipino remain under-represented and linguistically unexamined. Prior Filipino NLP evaluation resources suffered from fragmentation, limited task diversity, domain specificity, translationese bias from unverified automated translations, and poor handling of agglutinative morphology, syntactic word order variations (karaniwang ayos versus di-karaniwang ayos), and Taglish code-switching.
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Filipino and Tagalog-English Code-Switching (Taglish), Large Language Model Evaluation, Low-Resource Languages
theoretical_framework: Official Filipino linguistic and translation standards from the Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino (Almario, 2014, 2016); Filipino syntactic theory contrasting predicate-initial natural order (karaniwang ayos) with topicalized inverted order (di-karaniwang ayos / ay-inversion) and discourse continuity frameworks (Tanawan et al., 2008; Malicsi, 2013; Kroeger, 1993; Fox, 1985; Bolata, 2022); translationese theory (Gellerstam, 1986; Riley et al., 2020); and holistic multilingual language model benchmarking frameworks (HELM by Liang et al., 2023; BHASA by Leong et al., 2023; XTREME by Hu et al., 2020).
methodology: The authors developed BATAYAN, an eight-task benchmark evaluating LLMs across Natural Language Understanding (NLU: Paraphrase Identification, Question Answering, Sentiment Analysis, Toxicity Detection), Natural Language Reasoning (NLR: Causal Reasoning, Natural Language Inference), and Natural Language Generation (NLG: Abstractive Summarization, Machine Translation English-to-Filipino and Filipino-to-English). The curation workflow generated 3,800 test instances and five-shot exemplars through native translation using Helsinki-NLP OPUS-MT followed by human revision (PAWS, Balanced COPA, XNLI, XL-Sum), native re-translation of translated corpora (Belebele QA, FLORES-200 MT) to eliminate translationese bias and favor natural predicate-initial sentence order, and repurposing natively-sourced Philippine election tweets for sentiment analysis and toxicity detection. Dataset quality control applied three-rater native speaker consensus over binary criteria (completeness, fluency, sensibility) and multi-dimensional scaled criteria (faithfulness, relevance, coherence for summarization). The authors evaluated over 50 LLMs across small (<=11B), medium (<=32B), large (>=32B), and commercial model categories under zero-shot prompting for instruction-tuned models and five-shot prompting for base pre-trained models.
datasets: BATAYAN: An overarching benchmark containing 3,800 test instances across 8 tasks spanning NLU, NLR, and NLG competencies in Filipino and Taglish
PAWS (Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling): 400 test samples natively translated from English for Filipino Paraphrase Identification (PI)
Belebele: 100 test samples natively re-translated from machine-translated Filipino for Reading Comprehension Question Answering (QA)
Philippine Election Tweets (Cabasag et al., 2019): 600 test samples natively annotated for 3-class Sentiment Analysis (SA) and 400 test samples for Toxicity Detection (TD)
Balanced COPA (Choice of Plausible Alternatives): 400 test samples natively translated from English for Causal Reasoning (CR)
XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference): 600 test samples natively translated from English for Natural Language Inference (NLI)
XL-Sum: 100 test samples natively translated and manually summarized for Abstractive Summarization (AS)
FLORES-200: 1,200 test samples (600 English->Filipino, 600 Filipino->English) natively re-translated for Machine Translation (MT)

metrics: Macro F1 (NLU and NLR tasks: PI, QA, SA, TD, CR, NLI)
ROUGE-L F1 (Multilingual ROUGE implementation for Abstractive Summarization)
Cohen's Kappa and Krippendorff's Alpha (Inter-annotator agreement for Sentiment Analysis annotation)
Joint Agreement (Human acceptability judgment on completeness, fluency, and sensibility)

inter_annotator_agreement.quality_filtering: 3/3 rater unanimous joint agreement on binary criteria (completeness, fluency, sensibility)

key_findings: The authors created BATAYAN, a native-speaker-validated benchmark of 3,800 test instances across 8 tasks, introducing the first Filipino evaluation datasets for abstractive summarization, causal reasoning, and paraphrase identification.

Dedicated Filipino instruction tuning produces large performance gains on culturally and morphologically nuanced tasks; Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B-IT attained an average macro F1 of 79.23 on small-model NLU and 92.75 on causal reasoning, whereas non-adapted models such as Llama-3 variants scored near zero on causal reasoning.

Automated translations of English corpora exhibited systemic translationese bias, including an unnatural preference for inverted word order (di-karaniwang ayos / ay-inversion) and pragmatically awkward word choices, which native human re-translation corrected into natural predicate-initial constructions (karaniwang ayos).

Model performance exhibited clear scaling effects across parameter sizes (7B to 671B), demonstrating that greater model capacity combined with regional instruction tuning significantly improves the representation of agglutinative morphology, focus marking, and Taglish code-switching.

Open-source models with dedicated Filipino tuning (such as Gemma-SEA-LION-v3-9B-IT and Llama-SEA-LION-v3-70B-IT) achieved performance competitive with or superior to top commercial models (Gemini 1.5/2.0 and GPT-4o variants) on Filipino natural language understanding and reasoning tasks.

Semantic evaluation metrics such as MetricX-24 revealed significant translation quality advantages (MetricX-24 >87 for Filipino-tuned models) that surface-level lexical overlap metrics such as ROUGE-L failed to detect.
scope_and_delimitations: The benchmark focuses exclusively on Filipino (Tagalog) and Tagalog-English code-switched (Taglish) text, excluding other regional Philippine languages.

Task scope is delimited to eight specific NLP tasks: Paraphrase Identification, Question Answering, Sentiment Analysis, Toxicity Detection, Causal Reasoning, Natural Language Inference, Abstractive Summarization, and Machine Translation.

Benchmark volume is delimited to 3,800 high-quality test instances (100 to 1,200 samples per task) selected through strict unanimous three-rater acceptability criteria rather than large unverified web scrapes.
Social media data for sentiment analysis and toxicity detection is delimited to Philippine election-related tweets from 2019.
Model evaluation is delimited to zero-shot inference for instruction-tuned models and five-shot in-context learning for base pre-trained models.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt:
While our work provides a unique and comprehensive Filipino language benchmark, we also reported in previous sections the challenges and limitations in developing high-quality NLP resources for the under-represented language. Additionally, prosodic characteristics such as stress and sarcasm are not immediately obvious in the datasets utilized. We account for this by selecting only high-agreement samples. We also note that the domain of both SA and TD tasks (which were tweets surrounding political events), limits the distributions of these tasks, and as such we recommend utilizing other datasets that cover a wider set of domains and use cases.

While we recognize that datasets with larger amounts of samples are preferred to ensure generalizability, we maintain our position to prioritize consistent, high-quality, and representative samples.
limitations.summary: The authors identify several study limitations: prosodic features such as stress and sarcasm are difficult to identify in text datasets; sentiment analysis and toxicity detection corpora are restricted to political election tweets; total dataset size is delimited to 3,800 instances because the authors prioritized manual native quality filtering over dataset volume; and broad benchmark scope prevented comprehensive qualitative error analysis or evaluation on specialized translation models.

generalizability_gap: The benchmark evaluates only Filipino/Tagalog and Taglish text within written formats, leaving unexamined the more than 100 other Philippine regional languages (such as Cebuano, Ilocano, and Hiligaynon), spoken modalities, and non-political domain distributions for sentiment and toxicity tasks.
methodological_gap: Automated lexical evaluation metrics such as ROUGE-L lack sensitivity to semantic fidelity and morphological subtleties in agglutinative Filipino text; tools to automatically differentiate translationese from natural text remain unavailable; subjective stylistic preferences for sentence order (karaniwang ayos versus di-karaniwang ayos) introduce minor syntactic variance; and the study did not include comprehensive qualitative error category breakdowns.
future_work: Developing automated metrics and classification tools to discriminate translationese from natural Filipino text.
Expanding the benchmark to larger sample sizes, diverse non-political domains, and broader social media use cases.
Conducting detailed error analyses to characterize model failure modes across specific morphological and syntactic structures.
Evaluating specialized language models and extending benchmarking frameworks to other regional languages of the Philippines.
Maintaining and expanding the public evaluation suite and leaderboard on SEA-HELM for collaborative progress in Southeast Asian NLP.
